definition: Local spot markets differ in how much government controls pricing. A regulated market has prices set by government legislation, typically administered through a government-sponsored monopoly overseen by a regulatory commission, with relatively little trading. A deregulated market allows competitive pricing and was largely designed to encourage trading.
core_idea: The degree of government control over a local power market determines how much genuine trading activity that market supports.
key_points: Every municipality can set its own rules governing the physical delivery of power within its boundaries.
Regulated markets: government-sponsored monopoly, commission oversight, little trading.
Deregulated markets: competitive pricing, designed to encourage trading.
relationships: Local regulation is presented as a companion feature to the local/fragmented nature of spot markets
trading_implications: Trading opportunity is concentrated in deregulated markets; regulated markets offer little room for active trading due to administered pricing.
